title: Tulppa heikkenee: tulpat
subtitle: Consonant gradation — the sound-shift you've already been reading

blocks.text: Tulppa became tulpat in Lesson 10. Vika became viat in Lesson 3. Asiakas became asiakkaan in Lesson 12. Every one of those was hand-waved as 'a small shift' at the time. There's actually one unified system behind all three: consonant gradation, astevaihtelu. Today it finally gets a name and a shape.

blocks.title: Not an exception — a rule
blocks.text: Learners often mistake gradation for a pile of irregular words to memorise individually. It isn't. It's a predictable sound-softening that happens whenever certain endings (plurals, cases, possessive suffixes) get attached — the consonant in the middle of the word 'gives way' under the extra weight of the new ending, the same way English 'wife' softens to 'wives' before a plural.
Piece 1 — Double consonants weaken: pp → p

blocks.content: The clearest version: a double consonant like pp shrinks to a single p when certain endings attach. {Tulppa|grammar|strong grade|spark plug} (strong grade, standalone form) → {tulpat|grammar|weak grade|spark plugs} (weak grade, with the plural -t). The same thing happens with kk → k and tt → t across many other words — always double softening to single.

items.fi: Yksi {tulppa|grammar|strong grade|spark plug}, monta {tulpat|grammar|weak grade|spark plugs, plural}.
items.en: One spark plug, many spark plugs.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Sometimes the consonant vanishes: k → nothing

blocks.title: Vika → viat, the disappearing k
blocks.text: A single k between vowels can weaken all the way to nothing. {Vika|grammar|strong grade|fault} (strong grade) → {viat|grammar|weak grade|faults} (weak grade, plural) — the k simply drops out, leaving via + t. This looked like an irregular plural back in Lesson 3. It's actually the same gradation system, just taken one step further than pp → p.

items.fi: {Vika|grammar|strong grade|fault} löytyi nopeasti, mutta {viat|grammar|weak grade|faults} olivat useita.
items.en: The fault was found quickly, but there were several faults.

blocks.text: Piece 3 — Recognising it, not deriving it

blocks.content: You don't need to predict every gradation pair from scratch — even native speakers just know the pairs from hearing them constantly. What matters is recognising the pattern when you meet it, so a word like {asiakkaan|grammar|weak grade, genitive|of the customer} (Lesson 12) doesn't look like a random new word, but like asiakas wearing its expected weak grade for the genitive ending.

items.fi: {Asiakas|grammar|strong grade|customer} soitti, ja {asiakkaan|grammar|weak grade, genitive|the customer's} auto korjattiin.
items.en: The customer called, and the customer's car was fixed.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: How many spark plugs had to be changed?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Kaikki tulpat, ja lisäksi pari muuta vikaa löytyi.
lines.en: All the spark plugs, and a couple of other faults were found too.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Ei, mutta asiakkaan piti silti maksaa niistä kaikista.
lines.en: No, but the customer still had to pay for all of them.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: From now on, whenever a word looks like it's missing a letter compared to a form you already know — korjaamo staying put but tulppa losing a p, vika losing its whole k — check whether gradation explains it before assuming it's a new word. Nine times out of ten, it's a word you already own, just wearing its weak grade.

blocks.content: Tulppa vs tulpat: TULP-pa (double p held) vs TUL-pat (single p, lighter). Vika vs viat: VI-ka (clear k) vs VI-at (no k at all, just the vowel meeting the ending directly). Listen for the missing weight in the weak grade — that's the whole cue.

rows.en: spark plug / spark plugs (pp → p gradation)

blocks.title: What you now own
items: the name and shape of consonant gradation: astevaihtelu
the pp → p pattern: tulppa → tulpat
the k → nothing pattern: vika → viat
you can now look back at asiakkaan (Lesson 12) and see gradation instead of an irregular form
you have a general instinct for recognising gradation on sight, even in words you haven't met yet
